sub_sections.title: Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development
sub_sections.content:
## 2.1 Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

FIELDWISE is designed so that its scientific work programme and its career-development architecture are the same object seen from two sides: every advanced competence the research requires is also a competence the fellow needs in order to move to the next stage of an independent career. The action is a European Fellowship hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), with a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, over a total duration of 30 months (24 months at the host, M1-M24, plus the placement, M25-M30). This structure is used deliberately to deliver the MSCA-PF expected outcome of an increased set of research and transferable skills leading to improved employability and career prospects within academia and beyond (EO-01), and to substantiate the corresponding impact of improved researcher employability and career mobility within and outside academia (EI-01).

### Starting point and target trajectory

The fellow, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, is a plant physiologist whose foundation lies in agronomy, plant protection and plant physiology, combined with developing expertise in Earth observation, GIS and agricultural data science. The fellowship is deliberately positioned to convert this profile into a scarce and distinctive one. The intended career progression is explicit and staged: from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist, through EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist, to an Independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. FIELDWISE addresses the precise competence gap that stands between these stages — Bayesian modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor transfer, uncertainty, domain adaptation and decision evaluation — so that the measures below are not generic training but are targeted at named, missing capabilities the fellow can identify in her own record.

### Specific measures to develop advanced research skills

The scientific programme equips the fellow with advanced competence in Bayesian and probabilistic modelling, uncertainty quantification, spatio-temporal validation, sensor-domain transfer, cross-country adaptation, operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation, and IP and exploitation. These are acquired through supervised research practice on the project's own work packages rather than in the abstract: the prospective, uncertainty-aware prediction work develops the probabilistic-modelling and uncertainty competences; the temporal and cross-country transferability work develops the domain-adaptation and validation competences; and the operational-transfer work develops the decision-evaluation and research-to-MVP competences.

Skills development is genuinely bidirectional, which is the mechanism that makes it interdisciplinary rather than one-directional up-skilling. ELTE, through its remote-sensing group, transfers to the fellow geoinformatics, EO time-series analysis, optical/SAR integration, hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer, spatio-temporal modelling, Bayesian hierarchical modelling, uncertainty quantification, transfer learning and domain adaptation, reproducible geospatial computation, research software and web deployment, and IP and research exploitation. The fellow transfers to ELTE plant physiology, horticultural crop science, plant protection and agronomy, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping, hyperspectral field measurement and the biological interpretation of EO. The transfer therefore runs crop physiology and agronomy against geospatial and data science in both directions, which is exactly the international and interdisciplinary mind-set the call seeks to forge.

### The Career Development Plan as the governing instrument

The measures are made operational, auditable and time-bound through a Career Development Plan, submitted as deliverable D1.3 Career Development Plan and established jointly by the supervisors and the researcher, consistent with the call requirement that such a plan be agreed jointly and submitted early in the action. With a co-supervisor in place, joint establishment is taken to mean that the plan is signed by both supervisors and the fellow. The plan comprises six components: research objectives (O1 to O6); training and career needs; transferable skills; teaching; publications planning; and open-science engagement. Its progress is tracked as a measurable indicator — the plan is agreed by M3 and reviewed at all five steering points (M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27) — so that career development is monitored on the same cadence as the science, including a review point inside the placement window when non-academic career development is most in play.

The transferable-skills strand is concrete and mapped to the call's training obligations: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. These directly answer the requirement that fellowship training integrate key transferable and digital skills (including generative AI), Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and research integrity. Discipline-specific competences are delivered as eleven structured ELTE-to-fellow competences, provided through supervised practice supported by named ELTE courses rather than left to osmosis. The quality and intensity of supervision underpinning this are specified: a weekly one-to-one meeting between the fellow and supervisor Prof. András Jung; a weekly technical session with co-supervisor Dr. Roland Hollós through WP3 and WP4, who provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development while the fellow designs, builds and runs the models; a monthly written progress record held by the fellow; and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors.

### Measures to enhance employability outside academia — the non-academic placement

The single strongest employability measure is the six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR (M25-M30), which supplies the inter-sectoral half of the career progression that the academic host structurally cannot provide: operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation, and direct exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements. The placement is inside the company that operates the farms and the FMIS, so the fellow acquires these competences in the environment where they are actually exercised — the nine-dimension MVP assessment, farmer-field access and the FMIS integration roadmap all depend on the company's own operational and customer-facing setting. On-site supervision during the placement is provided by Miklós Maróti at senior research grade, and the fellow is embedded in the AgroVIR product development team responsible for the FMIS platform, so that the placement is a supervised research-training period and not an unstructured secondment. This is the segment of the profile that makes the fellow employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and farm-management-information-system providers as well as in academia, and it lets her demonstrate, on the record, that she has taken a scientific concept through the full chain from experimental evidence to validated model, to cross-country testing, to commercial-field testing, and to a working MVP — an end-to-end delivery experience that few academic-only postdoctoral profiles can claim.

### Teaching, networking and public-engagement measures

The plan builds a teaching and supervision record appropriate to an independent-researcher trajectory: the fellow co-designs and delivers a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, rather than a single guest lecture, and co-supervises the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. This is framed honestly as an existing strength transferred into a new setting rather than a competence acquired from zero: the fellow taught for five years at Agricultural University Plovdiv (2015-2020), including syllabus design, lecturing and examining in Bulgarian and English and Bachelor's thesis supervision, and the developmental content is the move to Earth-observation teaching in English at a Hungarian informatics faculty and the step up towards doctoral-level supervision. Networking and communication competences are developed through a defined publication programme (scientific outputs P1 to P4, with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship) and through public engagement beyond scientific peers, comprising one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers and one public-facing article per year, with science communication carried as one of the seven transferable-skill strands.

### Expected contribution to the future career of the researcher

Taken together, these measures create a distinctive scientific profile that combines biological understanding with scalable geospatial prediction and operational agricultural decision support — a combination that is uncommon precisely because it spans the physiology, the remote sensing and the deployment engineering that are usually held by different people. This profile is relevant to, and marketable across, European research institutes, universities, EU agricultural and environmental research, Earth-observation organisations, precision-agriculture companies, irrigation-technology providers and FMIS providers. The intended endpoint is the capacity for independent research in transferable agricultural intelligence, carried by an agreed and reviewed Career Development Plan; this is the researcher-level outcome the project commits to (OC6), and it is the concrete route by which FIELDWISE turns two years of research plus a six-month inter-sectoral placement into durably improved employability and career perspectives inside and outside academia.

sub_sections.title: Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities
sub_sections.content:
## 2.2 Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities

FIELDWISE is a single-researcher European Fellowship hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) with a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, and its measures to maximise outcomes and impacts are deliberately sized to that scale: they are built on the concrete outputs the work plan already produces rather than on a large stand-alone communication apparatus that one fellow could not credibly staff. The strategy separates three audiences and matches a distinct instrument to each — dissemination to scientific peers, exploitation towards operational users, and communication to the general public and the agricultural sector — while a common Open Science posture and an explicit intellectual-property allocation run underneath all three. Every measure below is tied to a named deliverable or to an operator-decided activity, and the eleven project KPIs give the whole plan measurable, checkable targets, so that the maximisation of impact is auditable rather than asserted. This design also directly answers the criticism recorded against a previous submission that the economic and technological route to users and the IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated.

### Dissemination to the scientific community

The scientific dissemination plan is organised around four principal publication outputs: P1 on the physiological and hyperspectral early-warning signatures of processing-tomato water stress; P2 on hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scaling for water-stress prediction; P3 on the temporal and cross-country transferability of agricultural water-stress models; and P4 on research-to-commercial transfer and the decision-oriented evaluation of agricultural AI. At least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions are targeted during or shortly after the fellowship, with submissions concentrated from the mid-fellowship steering point onward and aligned to the release of the key research assets. All peer-reviewed publications arising from the fellowship are made available in open access.

Beyond publications, dissemination is carried by three reusable research assets released openly for the community. The Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2) is released with a recorded transferability verdict against each candidate feature, so that Earth-observation and agricultural-AI research groups can reuse the feature-transfer methods directly; its completeness is tracked by KPI K2, which requires that every candidate hyperspectral feature carry an explicit transferable or hyperspectral-only verdict. The FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2) is released with a published model card, tracked by KPI K4, and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3) is published as a reusable output that states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to re-fit the model to a new agro-environment, tracked by KPI K6. The Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report (D4.2) is delivered to the international collaboration partner MVCRI — reported to Prof. Vinelina Yankova, who is not its author — and reports both zero-shot and locally calibrated performance, tracked by KPI K5. The target groups for this strand are therefore precise rather than generic: agricultural remote-sensing and geoinformatics researchers; plant-physiology and crop-stress modelling scientists working on transferable agricultural AI; Earth-observation and agricultural-AI groups reusing feature-transfer methods; research organisations and modelling teams adapting the engine to new regions, including MATE and MVCRI; and the wider cross-country agricultural-AI transfer community.

These dissemination measures maximise the call's expected outcomes for enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers (EO-03) and for stronger R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among participating organisations (EO-07), and they substantiate the corresponding scientific expected impact of enriched, more inter-connected European R&I (EI-02) and of increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer across European research organisations (EI-05), which the impact architecture maps to D2.2, D3.2 and D4.3.

### Open Science

The project follows the principle "as open as possible, as closed as necessary". Expected open outputs include the harmonisation protocols, the validation split manifests, the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, analysis and model code where IP permits, model cards, FAIR metadata, selected derived or anonymised datasets, and open-access publications. Research data is managed under FAIR curation (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) consistent with MSCA open-science practice, with a data-management plan foreseen early in the action. Open Science and FAIR practice, together with research integrity and generative-AI literacy, are carried explicitly as strands of the Career Development Plan (D1.3), so that open-science engagement is a trained competence and a monitored obligation rather than an afterthought. This directly serves the call requirement that fellowship training foster an Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and good scientific conduct.

### Exploitation towards operational uptake

The exploitation plan is what makes the operational-transfer half of FIELDWISE structural rather than asserted, and it is concentrated in WP5 Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP. Its spine is the advancement of the work from a desktop research prototype to a scientifically validated web MVP: the DrR web MVP (D5.1) is a reachable tool serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution, tracked by KPI K7. The MVP is then subjected to external functional and technical evaluation by the non-academic partner: the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4) assesses it against real agricultural-software requirements across all nine assessment dimensions, tracked by KPI K9, and supplies independent, end-user evidence on operational fitness and uptake readiness. The route beyond the fellowship is then made explicit by the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5), written from inside the implementing company, which names the required interfaces and the concrete post-fellowship steps for embedding the engine in farm-management information systems, tracked by KPI K10. Complementing the operational route, the Adaptation protocol (D4.3) provides the exploitation path into new growing regions by stating the minimum local-calibration cost of re-using the trained models elsewhere in Europe. Because the six-month placement is embedded in the company that operates the farms and the FMIS, the exploitation evidence is gathered where the technology would actually be used, which is the strongest available substantiation of the route to users. These measures maximise the call outcome of stronger knowledge transfer (EO-07) and evidence the technological and European expected impacts of the project.

### Communication to the public and the agricultural sector

Communication is aimed beyond scientific peers at two clearly identified public audiences. One public field demonstration is held with AgroVIR farmers — processing-tomato growers and farm operators in the AgroVIR farmer network, addressed as a public audience rather than as researchers — to show in-field how the tool supports irrigation timing and stress detection and to gather grower feedback. One public-facing article per year, written in accessible language for the interested public and the regional and agricultural-sector press, communicates the aims and results of the fellowship and raises public understanding of transferable agricultural AI for water-efficient farming. Science communication is one of the seven transferable-skill strands of the Career Development Plan, so the fellow is equipped to deliver these activities. These communication measures are the project's response to the call's expected impact of broadened public engagement with research and innovation (EI-03), for which the impact architecture records that the measures are operator-decided activities carrying no deliverable identifier of their own; they are stated here as commitments rather than attached to a fabricated dissemination deliverable.

### Management of intellectual property and foreseen protection measures

The exploitation posture is open by default, which is appropriate to the project's assets: the predictive engine is released with a published model card (D3.2), and the transfer library (D2.2) and adaptation protocol (D4.3) are published as reusable outputs, so exploitation proceeds primarily through open release and non-academic uptake rather than through formal protection. No patent or other formal protection is presently claimed. Should any protectable outcome be identified during the AgroVIR evaluation and the FMIS roadmap work (D5.4 and D5.5), it would be assessed jointly by the host and the partner before any disclosure, so that open dissemination and possible protection are reconciled deliberately rather than by omission. Responsibility for contract, finance, IP and open-access policy rests with the host, ELTE, escalating to the ELTE research office, so there is a single, unambiguous owner of IP decisions across the action.

A specific IP question arises from the placement, and it is addressed rather than left implicit: the fellow's own DrR — Digital Agronomist components are recorded as her background IP, and the six-month placement involves work on the prediction pipeline inside a commercial partner. The foreseen allocation is that ownership of placement results follows the grant agreement default, vesting in ELTE as the beneficiary acting through the fellow, and that a written placement agreement between the fellow, ELTE and AgroVIR, concluded before the placement begins, confirms this allocation and the access terms to the fellow's DrR background IP. This allocation is stated as a foreseen arrangement to be confirmed by that agreement, not as a settled fact, because the agreement does not yet exist. This treatment of the route to users and of IP is the direct remedy to the previous evaluation's finding that the economic and technological route to users and the IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated.

### Proportionality, and concrete actions during and after the project

The measures are proportionate to a single-fellow action and are concrete both during and after the fellowship. During the project, each strand is delivered through named deliverables on a defined schedule — the open transfer library and model card, the transferability report to MVCRI, the validated MVP and its external evaluation, the annual public-facing article and the in-field demonstration — and each is anchored to a KPI so that delivery can be verified rather than presumed. After the project, results persist through several durable, project-grounded channels: the released predictive engine with its published model card (D3.2) and the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5) together provide a maintained, integrable software asset and a concrete, partner-validated uptake path; the open transfer library (D2.2) and adaptation protocol (D4.3) allow other European regions to reuse and re-calibrate the methods at a stated minimum calibration cost; the integration of the research results into ELTE teaching — the co-designed and delivered module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture — carries the knowledge forward into education, serving the call's expected impact on the feedback of research into teaching (EI-06); and the reviewed Career Development Plan (D1.3) sustains the fellow's own capacity to continue the line of work. Responsibility for sustaining these results is distributed across ELTE, AgroVIR, MATE and MVCRI, so no single point of failure determines whether the impact outlives the fellowship. Taken together, the dissemination, exploitation and communication measures are matched in scale and specificity to what one fellow, one host and three associated partners can credibly deliver, and each is traceable to a project mechanism that produces it.

sub_sections.title: The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts
sub_sections.content:
## 2.3 The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

FIELDWISE is a single-researcher European Fellowship hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) with a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, and the importance of its results rests not on the size of the action but on the generality of what a small, tightly-scoped action can demonstrate. Where sub-section 2.1 concerns the fellow's own development and 2.2 concerns the machinery that carries the results to their audiences, this sub-section states how those results make a difference beyond their immediate scope — beyond one crop, one host institution and one growing season — and sizes that difference against the call's expected impacts, with quantified indicators wherever a credible and honest number is available. The project addresses a problem of genuine European magnitude: approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, referenced to the European Environment Agency, and climate change is expected both to increase the agricultural area requiring irrigation and to raise irrigation demand where irrigation is already practised, so that the timing of irrigation decisions is a lever on a continent-scale resource problem. FIELDWISE does not claim to solve that problem; it changes the way one class of decision-support technology is built, evaluated and transferred, and the value of that change is what the paragraphs below quantify. Each contribution is anchored to the project's eleven KPIs (K1 to K11), each of which fixes a verifiable target on a named project output, so that magnitude is asserted against measurable commitments rather than rhetorically.

### Scientific impact and its reach beyond the project

The project's primary scientific contribution is a framework for agricultural AI evaluated according to temporal, geographic and operational transferability rather than only retrospective accuracy, and, additionally, a methodological bridge between high-information proximal hyperspectral observations and scalable Sentinel-based prediction. The importance of this is that it is not confined to processing tomato or to the two study regions: the failure mode it corrects — models that score well on retrospective metrics such as R², RMSE or classification accuracy yet transfer poorly to new seasons, new regions and real farms — is generic to accuracy-centred agricultural machine learning, so a demonstrated, reusable alternative evaluation discipline is of interest to the wider agricultural remote-sensing and agricultural-AI community well beyond FIELDWISE's own experiments. The magnitude of this contribution is made concrete and durable by three openly released assets rather than by publications alone: the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2), released with an explicit transferable or hyperspectral-only verdict recorded against every candidate feature (K2); the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2), released with a published model card (K4) and reporting calibration and prediction-interval coverage at forecast horizons t+1, t+3 and t+5 (K3); and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3), which states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to re-fit the model to a new agro-environment (K6). These map directly to the call's expected impacts of an enriched, more inter-connected European R&I culture and of increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations, and the last of them — a stated minimum calibration cost — is precisely what converts a locally trained model into an asset other European groups can re-use at a known, bounded cost, which is the mechanism by which the scientific contribution propagates beyond the immediate scope.

### Economic and technological impact

The economic and technological importance of FIELDWISE lies in its deliberate advancement of the work from a desktop research prototype to a scientifically validated web MVP, and in the fact that its readiness for real use is judged not by the project itself but by an external, non-academic evaluator. The DrR web MVP (D5.1) is a reachable tool serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution (K7); the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4) assesses it against real agricultural-software requirements across all nine assessment dimensions (K9); and the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5) names the required interfaces and the concrete post-fellowship steps for embedding the engine in farm-management information systems (K10). The importance of this chain is that it makes the route to economic uptake explicit and independently tested rather than asserted, which is the specific remedy to the previous submission's finding that the economic and technological route to users was insufficiently substantiated. The economic relevance of the target problem is itself substantial: water scarcity already produces agricultural yield losses and higher water costs in Europe, irrigation demand is expected to increase under climate change, and processing tomato is a high-value horticultural crop in which improved irrigation timing can therefore carry substantial agronomic and economic relevance. The magnitude of the available exploitation channel is unusually favourable for a single-fellow action because the non-academic partner is not a laboratory but a company whose farm-management information system is reported to be in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria — the two countries FIELDWISE works in — so the roadmap it writes from inside the implementing company points at an existing operational footprint rather than a hypothetical market. This substantiates the call's expected impact of strengthened R&I competitiveness and knowledge-transfer capacity of participating organisations; it is presented as the scale of the route to users, not as a promise of adoption within the fellowship, which the project explicitly does not make.

### Societal and environmental impact

The societal and environmental contribution follows from the same mechanism seen from the public side. By improving the timing and spatial prioritisation of irrigation decisions, FIELDWISE contributes to the EU-level opportunity for water savings in irrigated agriculture. Importantly, and as a matter of credibility rather than modesty, the project does not claim in advance that it will achieve a particular percentage reduction in water use; the environmental benefit will be quantified from project evidence rather than pre-declared. This discipline is deliberate: an MSCA-PF action with one fellow and a 30-month horizon cannot honestly commit to a headline water-saving number, and stating one would weaken rather than strengthen the impact case. What the project can commit to, and does, is the field-level measurement that makes any later saving assessable — the Field Decision Value report (D5.3) computes decision value for at least two competing models and reports lead time, false action rate and missed stress rate (K8), so that model choice is driven by operational usefulness rather than retrospective fit. Beyond the environmental route, the societal reach of the action is broadened by two public-facing measures the project commits to as activities: one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers and one public-facing article per year, which serve the call's expected impact of broadened public engagement with research and innovation and which, being operator-decided activities, carry no deliverable identifier of their own. The results are also carried into education through the co-design and delivery of a module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, serving the expected impact on the feedback of research results into teaching; and, at the level of the individual researcher, the fellowship's contribution to improved employability and career mobility within and beyond academia — carried by the Career Development Plan (D1.3) and the inter-sectoral placement, and argued in full in 2.1 — feeds the call's broader societal aim of a more dynamic and flexible European research talent base. Convergence of researcher working conditions with the European Charter for Researchers is evidenced at instrument level by the Career Development Plan (D1.3) and by ELTE's recruitment and researcher-development policies; no HR Excellence in Research accreditation is claimed.

### The European dimension and replicability

The distinctively European importance of FIELDWISE is that its architecture directly investigates whether agricultural AI developed in one European environment can be transferred to another. The MATE-to-MVCRI design tests this concretely — the Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report (D4.2) reports both zero-shot and locally calibrated performance (K5) — but the contribution reaches past these two sites, because the question it answers is the general one of how locally developed agricultural intelligence can become reliably transferable rather than remaining confined to the field in which it was trained. This is why the Adaptation protocol (D4.3), by stating the minimum local calibration required to move the model to a new agro-environment, is as much a European-impact instrument as a scientific one: it turns a Hungary-to-Bulgaria result into a re-usable recipe for adaptation to other European growing regions, so the magnitude of the contribution is bounded below by the two tested regions and, through the protocol, extensible to others at a stated cost. The cross-country, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary character of the action — international transfer with MVCRI, inter-sectoral evaluation and placement with AgroVIR, and the two-way transfer between plant physiology and geoinformatics between the fellow and ELTE — is exactly the profile the call associates with strengthened European research collaboration.

### Magnitude, importance and the discipline of the quantified claim

Taken together, the project's contribution is proportionate to a single-fellow action yet structured so that its importance is not: the transferability-first evaluation framework, the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel bridge, the reusable transfer library, model card and adaptation protocol, the externally evaluated MVP and the named FMIS integration route are each designed to outlive the fellowship and to be picked up by others. The magnitude of each claim is disciplined by an explicit KPI, so an evaluator can check the commitment rather than take the ambition on trust: five integrated seasons (K1), an explicit transferability verdict on every candidate feature (K2), three evaluated forecast horizons (K3), a published model card (K4), a reported zero-shot and calibrated cross-country gap (K5), a stated adaptation cost (K6), a reachable MVP (K7), decision value computed for at least two models (K8), a nine-dimension external evaluation (K9), a defined integration path (K10), and a career plan agreed and reviewed on a fixed cadence (K11). Where a number would be credible and meaningful — the extent of European water scarcity, the horizons at which forecasts are issued, the dimensions on which the tool is externally assessed, the operational footprint of the exploitation channel — the project states it; where a number could only be guessed — the eventual water saving — it refuses to pre-commit and instead builds the measurement that will supply the number honestly. That combination of demonstrable reach and refusal to over-claim is the substance of FIELDWISE's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts.

The Adaptation protocol (D4.3) is published as a reusable output stating the minimum local-calibration volume, tracked by KPI K6.
The Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report (D4.2) is delivered to MVCRI (reported to Prof. Vinelina Yankova) with zero-shot and locally calibrated performance, tracked by KPI K5.
The dissemination target groups are the named research communities (agricultural remote sensing, geoinformatics, crop-stress modelling, EO/agricultural-AI reuse groups, MATE and MVCRI).

The project follows Open Science 'as open as possible, as closed as necessary' with the listed open outputs (protocols, split manifests, methodology, code where IP permits, model cards, FAIR metadata, derived data, open-access publications).
Research data is managed under FAIR curation consistent with MSCA open-science practice, with a data-management plan foreseen early in the action.
Open Science/FAIR, research integrity and generative-AI literacy are carried as strands of the Career Development Plan (D1.3), satisfying the call training requirement.

The DrR web MVP (D5.1) advances the work from a desktop prototype to a validated web MVP serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution, tracked by KPI K7.
The AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4) evaluates the MVP against real agricultural-software requirements across nine assessment dimensions, tracked by KPI K9.
The FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5) names required interfaces and post-fellowship steps for embedding the engine in farm-management information systems, tracked by KPI K10.
The plan addresses the previous evaluation's criticism that the economic/technological route to users and the IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated.

Communication comprises one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers and one public-facing article per year, addressed to growers and the interested public/agricultural-sector press, answering expected impact EI-03.
The IP posture is open by default with no formal protection presently claimed; any protectable outcome from D5.4/D5.5 is assessed jointly by host and partner before disclosure.
The fellow's DrR - Digital Agronomist components are recorded as her background IP, raising the ownership question the placement work addresses.

Ownership of placement results follows the grant agreement default, vesting in ELTE as the beneficiary acting through the fellow; a written placement agreement between the fellow, ELTE and AgroVIR, concluded before the placement begins, will confirm this allocation and the access terms to the fellow's DrR background IP.
Responsibility for contract, finance, IP and open-access policy rests with the host ELTE, escalating to the ELTE research office.

Results are sustained after the project via D3.2, D5.5, the open D2.2/D4.3 reuse path, ELTE teaching integration (module unit), and the reviewed Career Development Plan (D1.3), across ELTE, AgroVIR, MATE and MVCRI.
Integration of results into ELTE teaching (co-designed module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture) serves expected impact EI-06.
The dissemination/exploitation activities maximise the call expected outcomes EO-03 and EO-07 and expected impacts EI-02 and EI-05.
Each strand is anchored to a named deliverable and a KPI, giving verifiable delivery during the project and durable channels after it, proportionate to the action's scale.

FIELDWISE's primary scientific contribution is a framework for agricultural AI evaluated by temporal, geographic and operational transferability rather than only retrospective accuracy, plus a methodological bridge from proximal hyperspectral observation to scalable Sentinel-based prediction.

The project contributes to the EU-level opportunity for water savings by improving irrigation timing and spatial prioritisation, and deliberately does not pre-claim a percentage water reduction; the benefit is to be quantified from project evidence.

Water scarcity already causes yield losses and higher water costs while irrigation demand is rising, and processing tomato is a high-value crop in which improved timing carries substantial agronomic and economic relevance.

The project advances the work from a desktop research prototype to a scientifically validated web MVP, with external AgroVIR evaluation providing evidence on whether the technology meets real agricultural-software requirements.

The MATE-MVCRI architecture investigates whether agricultural AI developed in one European environment can transfer to another, contributing to the wider European question of making locally developed agricultural intelligence reliably transferable.
Approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, with irrigation demand and irrigated area expected to rise under climate change.

claim_statuses.claim_summary: The scientific dissemination assets map to the call's expected impacts of an enriched, more inter-connected European R&I culture (EI-02) and increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations (EI-05).

Three openly released assets — the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2), the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2) and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3) — carry the scientific contribution beyond the project, tracked by KPIs K2, K3, K4 and K6.
The Adaptation protocol (D4.3) states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to re-fit the model to a new agro-environment, enabling reuse by other European regions at a stated cost.

The DrR web MVP (D5.1, K7), the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation across nine assessment dimensions (D5.4, K9) and the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5, K10) make the economic/technological route to users explicit and externally tested.
The externally tested MVP-to-FMIS chain is the specific remedy to the previous submission's finding that the economic and technological route to users was insufficiently substantiated.

No participation in EU-funded research projects. AgroVIR's relevant track record is commercial rather than scientific: twenty years of practice in Hungarian commercial agriculture, and a farm management information system in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria — the two countries FIELDWISE works in.

The Field Decision Value report (D5.3) computes decision value for at least two competing models and reports lead time, false action rate and missed stress rate (K8), making later water/environmental benefit assessable.

Two public-facing measures — one public field demonstration with AgroVIR farmers and one public-facing article per year — serve the call's expected impact of broadened public engagement (EI-03) and carry no deliverable identifier of their own.
Co-design and delivery of a module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture serves the expected impact of feedback of research results into teaching (EI-06).

The fellowship's contribution to improved researcher employability and career mobility within and beyond academia, carried by the Career Development Plan (D1.3) and the placement, feeds the societal aim of a more dynamic European research talent base (EI-01).

Convergence of working conditions with the European Charter for Researchers is evidenced by the Career Development Plan (D1.3) and ELTE policies, with no HR Excellence in Research accreditation claimed.
The Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report (D4.2) reports both zero-shot and locally calibrated performance (K5), concretely testing cross-European transfer.

The project's magnitude is disciplined by eleven KPIs (K1 to K11), each fixing a verifiable target on a named output, including five integrated seasons, forecast horizons t+1/t+3/t+5, and a nine-dimension external evaluation.

The action's international (MVCRI), inter-sectoral (AgroVIR) and interdisciplinary (physiology-geoinformatics, fellow-ELTE) character matches the collaboration profile the call associates with strengthened European research collaboration.
